analysis.title: THINK Ahead: The AI-inflation tug of war that's driving markets crazy
key_insights: US rates swung sharply this week: hot CPI and PPI pushed two-year swap rates up 20 basis points, then the move fully reversed within hours on news of trouble at GPU cloud provider CoreWeave. ING calls it almost an entire rate hike priced in and out in hours.

The central question in US rates is why the Fed is hiking: persistent inflation worsened by the Middle East crisis, or AI-driven investment making financial conditions too loose. Fed officials do not agree on this.

Both consumer and producer price inflation surprised to the upside this week, with no single area clearly skewing the numbers higher. The three-month annualised rate of headline CPI is back above 3%, per James Knightley.

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's favoured gauge, the share of CPI components with inflation above 3%, remains very elevated but a little lower than before. ING considers the measure flawed because it mostly reflects tariffs lifting many small, low-weight goods categories.
ING expects the tariff effect to fade quickly as tariff refunds flow following the Supreme Court decision earlier this year.

Rents are 44% of the core inflation basket and should keep easing gradually given the cool US housing market. Wage growth is 3% and could fall further. ING sees inflation much closer to 2% by Q2 2027, when the energy effect drops out of annual comparisons.
AI investment is estimated by James Knightley to have contributed about a third of US economic growth so far this year, and AI companies appear indifferent to higher capital costs.

Warsh said in September that the Fed was 'removing a dose of accommodation', which ING reads as a sign he does not see policy as particularly restrictive. With Treasury yields above 5% and a stronger dollar tightening conditions, ING infers his concern about loose conditions is about the US equity market.
The health of the AI trade matters for the Fed's ability both to raise rates further and to hold them high for any period, which is why the CoreWeave news moved rates.

Outside AI, the US economy is weak: capital investment outside the data centre boom has barely grown in nearly two years, and financial stress in the bottom half of the income distribution is emerging in debt-servicing ratios and delinquencies. ING warns the Fed risks setting rates for the AI economy while the rest of the country is squeezed.
ING's call: the Fed hikes only once more, in December, and could cut again as soon as late 2027.

US week ahead: housing starts and flash PMIs are unlikely to move markets, and the Fed is in its blackout period ahead of the 28 October FOMC. Pricing shows about a 30% chance of a hike, with 9 December seen as the most likely date. ING agrees.

Canada: September CPI due Monday. ING expects 0.3% m/m and 3.3% y/y, which would likely leave the Bank of Canada leaning hawkish for the 28 October meeting with December kept open. Only an especially hot print would move markets toward a hike on 28 October.
Eurozone: ING expects October flash PMIs to fall on higher energy prices and France's budget difficulties, with the composite staying above 50.

UK: ING expects headline CPI to rise to 3.5%, heading toward 4% around the turn of the year. It expects the Bank of England to hike in November and probably February, but doubts rates will rise as far as markets price or stay high, and expects cuts by end-2027.

tension_points.bull_case: If hikes are about inflation, the Fed need not panic: tariff effects are fading with refunds, rents (44% of core) are easing, wage growth is 3%, and inflation should be near 2% by Q2 2027.
tension_points.bear_case: If hikes are about loose financial conditions from the AI boom, the Fed may need to hike further and hold longer; CPI and PPI surprised higher and 3-month annualised headline CPI is above 3%.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A further sell-off in the AI trade, as in the CoreWeave news, would undercut the Fed's ability to raise and hold rates.

theme_stances.key_argument: The Fed can get away with hiking only once more in December because inflation pressures should fade and the non-AI economy is weak.
